summary: Specifies algorithm identifiers and ASN.1 encodings for digital signatures and subject public keys used in the Internet X.509 PKI. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3279 gives certificates and certificate revocation lists standard names and formats for cryptographic algorithms and public keys. This lets different systems read the same certificate fields consistently.

questions: what oid does rsa use in a certificate
how are ecdsa public keys encoded in certificates
subtitle: The identifiers and encodings X.509 certificates use for public keys and signatures.

tldr.problem: Certificates and revocation lists need a shared way to identify the algorithms used to sign them and the public keys they contain.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3279 assigns object identifiers and defines ASN.1 encodings and parameter rules for hash, signature, and public-key algorithms used with the X.509 profile.
tldr.outcome: It supplements RFC 3280. It is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 4055, RFC 4491, RFC 5480, RFC 5758, and RFC 8692.

today: RFC 3279 is a Proposed Standard that supplements RFC 3280. It has been updated by RFC 4055, RFC 4491, RFC 5480, RFC 5758, and RFC 8692.

sections.title: What the Profile Defines
sections.content:
RFC 3279 supplements RFC 3280, the Internet X.509 certificate and certificate revocation list (CRL) profile. It defines the contents of four certificate and CRL fields: signatureAlgorithm, signatureValue, signature, and subjectPublicKeyInfo.

The profile names hash and signature algorithms and specifies how public keys are represented. It covers RSA, DSA, Diffie-Hellman, KEA, ECDSA, and ECDH keys, as well as RSA, DSA, and ECDSA signatures. A conforming implementation must also follow RFC 3280.

Certificate authorities and applications must support at least one of the specified signature and public-key algorithms. When they use an algorithm from this profile, they must support it as described here.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC defines how certificates name algorithms and write public keys and signatures. Systems that follow the same rules can interpret those fields in the same way.

sections.title: Hash Functions
sections.content:
A hash function reduces data to a fixed-size value called a message digest. The profile includes MD2, MD5, and SHA-1. It names SHA-1 as the preferred hash function for this profile and records MD2 and MD5 because existing uses depend on them.

MD2 and MD5 each produce a 128-bit hash, while SHA-1 produces a 160-bit hash. The RFC discourages MD2 and MD5 for new applications but says they may still be used to verify existing signatures. Its descriptions of these algorithms and their security reflect the document's publication period.
sections.plainLanguage: A hash is a short value calculated from data. This profile includes three hash methods and identifies SHA-1 as its preferred choice; it keeps MD2 and MD5 for checking older signatures.

sections.title: Signature Names and Encodings
sections.content:
A certificate or CRL identifies its signing method with an object identifier (OID) in signatureAlgorithm. The identifier may include parameters. The signature itself is formatted for the chosen algorithm, encoded as an ASN.1 BIT STRING, and placed in the signed object.

For RSA, the profile defines signatures combining RSA with MD2, MD5, or SHA-1. Their AlgorithmIdentifier parameters must be ASN.1 NULL. DSA and ECDSA signatures use SHA-1 in this profile, and their algorithm identifiers omit the parameters field.

DSA and ECDSA each produce two integer values, r and s. The profile encodes each pair as a sequence of two ASN.1 integers. For DSA and ECDSA verification, the issuer's public-key parameters apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate names the method that made its signature. The profile also fixes how each method's settings and signature values are written, so a verifier can interpret them consistently.

sections.title: Public-Key Names and Parameters
sections.content:
The subjectPublicKeyInfo field identifies a public-key algorithm with an OID and, when needed, parameters. A certificate authority must use the identifiers specified here, and an application supporting one of these key types must recognize its identifier.

RSA keys use the rsaEncryption identifier, a NULL parameter, and an ASN.1 sequence containing the modulus and public exponent. DSA keys use id-dsa and may carry domain parameters; if required DSA parameters are absent and cannot be obtained elsewhere, clients must reject the certificate. Diffie-Hellman keys include domain parameters, while KEA certificates carry an 80-bit domain identifier.

ECDSA and ECDH keys use id-ecPublicKey. Their curve parameters can be included in the certificate, named by an OID, or inherited from the issuer. Implementations supporting elliptic-curve keys must support uncompressed points; compressed points are optional.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate labels the kind of public key it contains and gives any settings that key needs. Elliptic-curve settings can be written out, named, or inherited from the issuer.

sections.title: The ASN.1 Module
sections.content:
The RFC gathers the identifiers and data structures into an ASN.1 module named PKIX1Algorithms88. ASN.1 describes structured data, while Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) provide a defined byte representation for many of those values.

The module lists identifiers and structures for the hash functions and supported key and signature algorithms. It also lists named elliptic curves: 20 characteristic-two curves and seven prime curves. These definitions provide a machine-readable form of the profile's encodings.
sections.plainLanguage: The final module collects the names and data layouts in a form software can process. It also lists the named elliptic curves included in the profile.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC does not set public-key sizes or choose particular elliptic curves. Those choices affect the strength of the cryptographic services, so implementers must select suitable sizes and curves.

The document recommends well-known curves, including named curves from ANSI X9.62, and says the security considerations in RFC 3280 also apply. Its algorithm discussion describes the profile at the time it was published.
sections.plainLanguage: The format rules do not guarantee that every key or curve is strong. Implementers must choose suitable parameters, and the related certificate profile's security guidance also applies.
